note: Topic codes, titles, unit structure, HL-only flags and teaching hours are factual features of the syllabus. All study content (essentials, diagrams, traps) is EconIB original writing.

topics.title: What is economics?
essentials: Scarcity: finite resources against unlimited wants, which forces the three basic questions — what to produce, how, and for whom.
Opportunity cost as the value of the next best alternative forgone.
Factors of production: land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship, and the income each earns (rent, wages, interest, profit).
The production possibilities curve: points on it are efficient, inside are unemployed resources, outside are unattainable; the curve's shape shows increasing opportunity cost.
Economic systems: free market, planned, and mixed — and where real economies sit between them.
The circular flow of income between households and firms, with injections and leakages.
diagrams: Production possibilities curve, including a shift outward for growth
topics.trap: Opportunity cost is the NEXT BEST alternative forgone, singular — not the sum of everything you gave up.

topics.title: How do economists approach the world?
essentials: Economics as a social science: models simplify by holding other things constant (ceteris paribus).
Positive statements (testable against evidence) versus normative statements (value judgments about what ought to be).
The nine key concepts as the conceptual thread running through the whole course.
Different schools of thought disagree about how markets self-correct, which is why evaluation is possible at all.
Equity and sustainability as central lenses on modern economic problems.
topics.trap: 'The government should raise the minimum wage' is normative. 'Raising the minimum wage above equilibrium creates a surplus of labour' is positive. Examiners ask you to distinguish these.

topics.title: Demand
essentials: The law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls, ceteris paribus.
Why the demand curve slopes down: income effect, substitution effect, and the law of diminishing marginal utility.
Non-price determinants: income, tastes and preferences, prices of substitutes and complements, expectations, number of consumers.
Movement ALONG the curve is caused by price; a SHIFT of the curve is caused by everything else.
Individual demand versus market demand as the horizontal sum.
diagrams: Movement along versus shift of the demand curve
hl: Assumptions behind the law of demand, including diminishing marginal utility
Linear demand functions: Qd = a - bP, and plotting them
topics.trap: 'Demand fell' and 'quantity demanded fell' are different claims. Price changes never shift the demand curve. This single confusion costs more marks than any other in Unit 2.

topics.title: Supply
essentials: The law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
Non-price determinants: costs of factors of production, prices of related goods (joint and competitive supply), indirect taxes and subsidies, expectations, technology, number of firms.
Movement along versus shift, exactly as with demand.
Individual firm supply versus market supply.
diagrams: Movement along versus shift of the supply curve
hl: The law of diminishing marginal returns and increasing marginal costs as the reason supply slopes up
Linear supply functions: Qs = c + dP
topics.trap: An indirect tax shifts supply LEFT (or upward by the tax per unit) — it is a cost to the producer, not a change in demand.

topics.title: Competitive market equilibrium
essentials: Equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; excess demand (shortage) below it and excess supply (surplus) above it.
How shifts in demand or supply produce a new equilibrium price and quantity.
Functions of the price mechanism: signalling, incentive, and rationing.
Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and social (community) surplus.
Allocative efficiency at the competitive equilibrium: community surplus is maximised where marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
diagrams: Changes in equilibrium and the price mechanism at work
hl: Calculating consumer and producer surplus from a diagram
Solving for equilibrium algebraically from demand and supply functions
topics.trap: Allocative efficiency is MB = MC, not simply 'where the curves cross'. State the condition; the free mark is in the wording.

topics.title: Critique of the maximizing behaviour of consumers and producers
essentials: The rational consumer assumption of standard theory: perfect information, utility maximisation, consistent preferences.
Behavioural critiques: biases and rules of thumb, bounded rationality, bounded self-control, imperfect information.
Choice architecture and nudge theory as policy tools.
Firms may pursue objectives other than profit maximisation — market share, growth, corporate social responsibility, satisficing.
topics.trap: This topic is a gift for evaluation anywhere in the course. If a question assumes rational behaviour, questioning that assumption is a legitimate and well-credited evaluative move.

topics.title: Elasticity of demand
essentials: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price; interpret the value, ignoring the negative sign.
Ranges: elastic (>1), inelastic (<1), unit elastic (=1), and the perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic extremes.
Determinants of PED: number and closeness of substitutes, degree of necessity, proportion of income spent, time.
PED and total revenue: raising price raises revenue when demand is inelastic and cuts it when elastic.
YED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in income; positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods, above 1 for luxuries.
Applications: why primary commodity producers face volatile incomes, and why the primary sector shrinks as economies develop.
diagrams: Relatively elastic and relatively inelastic demand
Perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic and unit elastic demand
hl: PED varies along a straight-line demand curve — it is not constant
Engel curves for income elastic, income inelastic and inferior goods
Calculating PED and YED from data
topics.trap: PED is not the slope. A single straight demand curve has elastic, unit elastic and inelastic sections. Saying 'the flatter curve is more elastic' is only true when comparing at the same price and quantity.

topics.title: Elasticity of supply
essentials: PES = % change in quantity supplied / % change in price.
Determinants: time, mobility of factors of production, spare capacity, ability to store stock, and the length of the production period.
Primary commodities tend to have low PES; manufactured goods higher.
diagrams: Relatively elastic and relatively inelastic supply
Perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic supply
hl: Calculating PES from data
topics.trap: Time is the dominant determinant. Almost all supply is more elastic in the long run, and saying so is an easy evaluation point in any tax or subsidy question.

topics.title: Role of government in microeconomics
essentials: Indirect taxes (specific and ad valorem): effect on price, quantity, consumer and producer surplus, government revenue, and welfare loss.
Subsidies: effect on price, quantity, government cost, and welfare.
Price ceilings (maximum prices) set below equilibrium: shortages, rationing, parallel markets, and welfare loss.
Price floors (minimum prices) set above equilibrium: surpluses, government buying, and welfare loss.
Minimum wage as a price floor in the labour market.
Tax incidence: the burden splits according to the relative elasticities of demand and supply.
diagrams: Specific and ad valorem indirect taxes
Price ceiling with shortage and welfare loss
Price floor with surplus and welfare loss
hl: Calculating from a diagram: tax revenue, subsidy cost, consumer and producer expenditure, and welfare loss
topics.trap: A price ceiling only binds if it is set BELOW equilibrium, and a price floor only if ABOVE. A non-binding control changes nothing — examiners set this deliberately.

topics.title: Market failure — externalities and common pool resources
essentials: Externalities as costs or benefits falling on third parties, so private and social costs or benefits diverge.
The four cases: negative production, positive production, negative consumption, positive consumption externalities.
Marginal private cost/benefit versus marginal social cost/benefit, and the welfare loss triangle.
Common pool resources: rivalrous but non-excludable, leading to over-use — the tragedy of the commons.
Policy responses: indirect taxes, carbon taxes, tradable permits, legislation and regulation, education, subsidies, direct provision, collective self-governance.
Sustainability and the need for international cooperation, and why enforcement is hard.
diagrams: Negative production externality with welfare loss
Positive consumption externality with welfare loss
hl: Calculating welfare loss from a diagram
topics.trap: Draw the welfare loss triangle and shade it. Many answers describe the externality perfectly and never show the loss, which caps criterion A and the diagram dimension of the markband.

topics.title: Market failure — public goods
essentials: Public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable.
The free rider problem means the private market will under-provide or not provide them at all.
Government responses: direct provision funded by taxation, or contracting out to the private sector.
topics.trap: 'Public good' does not mean 'good provided by the government'. Test both properties. Healthcare and education are usually merit goods, not public goods.

topics.title: Market failure — asymmetric information
essentials: Asymmetric information exists where one party to a transaction knows more than the other.
Adverse selection occurs before the transaction — the used car and insurance markets are the standard cases.
Moral hazard occurs after it, once behaviour changes because someone else bears the risk.
Government responses: legislation, regulation, provision of information.
Private responses: signalling by the informed party and screening by the uninformed.
hl: Entire topic is HL only
topics.trap: Adverse selection is before the deal, moral hazard after. Getting them the wrong way round is the most common HL slip here.

topics.title: Market failure — market power
essentials: Costs: fixed and variable, total and average, and marginal cost; the short run versus the long run.
Diminishing marginal returns in the short run; economies and diseconomies of scale in the long run.
Revenue: total, average and marginal, and how they differ under price-taking and price-making.
Profit maximisation at MC = MR; normal and abnormal profit; the shut-down and break-even rules.
Perfect competition: many firms, homogeneous products, free entry, price takers; allocative and productive efficiency in the long run.
Monopoly: barriers to entry, price making, abnormal profit sustained in the long run, welfare loss; natural monopoly.
Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, some price-setting power, no long-run abnormal profit.
Oligopoly: few firms, interdependence, collusion and cartels, game theory and the prisoner's dilemma, non-price competition.
Policy responses to market power: regulation, legislation, nationalisation, trade liberalisation.
diagrams: Perfect competition: firm and industry, short run and long run
Monopolistic competition, short run and long run
hl: Entire topic is HL only
Calculating costs, revenues and profit from data
topics.trap: MC cuts AC and AVC at their minimum points, always. Drawing it otherwise loses marks before the argument is read.

topics.title: The market's inability to achieve equity
essentials: Markets allocate on ability to pay, which need not produce a fair distribution.
Merit goods are under-consumed and demerit goods over-consumed relative to what is socially desirable.
The efficiency versus equity trade-off in policy design.
Government responses and their costs, including the incentive effects of redistribution.
hl: Entire topic is HL only
topics.trap: Equity is normative. Say whose conception of fairness you are applying — that acknowledgement is exactly what the top evaluation band rewards.

topics.title: Measuring economic activity and illustrating its variations
essentials: The circular flow of income, including injections (investment, government spending, exports) and leakages (saving, taxation, imports).
GDP measured three ways — output, income, expenditure — and why they are equal.
GDP versus GNI, and nominal versus real; why real figures are needed for comparison over time.
GDP per capita, and purchasing power parity for comparison across countries.
Limitations of national income statistics: the informal economy, unpaid work, externalities, distribution, and quality of life.
Alternative measures: the OECD Better Life Index, the Happy Planet Index, and the concept of green GDP.
The business cycle: expansion, peak, contraction, trough, and the long-term growth trend.
diagrams: Business cycle showing the trend line
hl: Calculating nominal and real GDP and GNI from data
Calculating GDP using a price deflator
topics.trap: Real GDP per capita is the figure that speaks to living standards. Quoting total nominal GDP growth in a development answer is a weak argument that examiners routinely penalise.

topics.title: Variations in economic activity — aggregate demand and aggregate supply
essentials: AD = C + I + G + (X − M), and the determinants of each component.
Why the AD curve slopes down: wealth, interest rate and international trade effects.
Short-run aggregate supply and its determinants (costs of production, indirect taxes, subsidies).
Two models of long-run supply: the monetarist/new classical vertical LRAS at full employment, and the Keynesian AS curve with its horizontal, upward-sloping and vertical sections.
Equilibrium: inflationary and deflationary (recessionary) gaps.
The multiplier effect and how a change in an injection produces a larger change in national income.
hl: Calculating the multiplier from MPC, MPS, MPT and MPM
Using the multiplier to find the change in real GDP
topics.trap: Choose your AS model deliberately and say why. The Keynesian and new classical models give different answers about whether the economy self-corrects — that choice IS the evaluation.

topics.title: Macroeconomic objectives
essentials: Low unemployment: measurement by the unemployment rate, and its limitations (hidden unemployment, underemployment, participation).
Types of unemployment: structural, frictional, seasonal, and cyclical (demand-deficient), with their different causes and cures.
Costs of unemployment, economic and social.
Low and stable inflation: measurement by CPI and its limitations.
Demand-pull and cost-push inflation; the costs of inflation and of deflation; disinflation.
Economic growth: actual versus potential, shown on a PPC or AD/AS diagram.
Conflicts between objectives, including the short-run Phillips curve trade-off between unemployment and inflation.
diagrams: Actual and potential growth on a PPC and on AD/AS
hl: Constructing a weighted price index and calculating inflation from it
Calculating the unemployment rate
topics.trap: Deflation and disinflation are not the same. Deflation is a falling price level; disinflation is a falling rate of inflation with prices still rising.

topics.title: Economics of inequality and poverty
essentials: Inequality of income and of wealth, and why the two differ.
The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient as measures.
Absolute versus relative poverty, and the difficulty of drawing a poverty line.
Causes of inequality and poverty: inheritance, discrimination, unequal education and health, unequal status and power.
Consequences: lower living standards, lower growth, reduced social cohesion.
Redistribution policies: progressive taxation, transfer payments, provision of merit goods, and universal basic income.
The equity versus efficiency trade-off in redistribution.
diagrams: Lorenz curve and the line of equality
Progressive, proportional and regressive tax structures
hl: Calculating the Gini coefficient conceptually from a Lorenz curve
Calculating marginal and average tax rates from a tax schedule
topics.trap: A higher Gini coefficient means MORE inequality. The Lorenz curve bows further from the 45-degree line. Reversing this reverses your whole argument.

topics.title: Demand management — monetary policy
essentials: The central bank's goals and its independence.
The interest rate as the main tool, and how it is set to influence AD.
The transmission mechanism: interest rates affect consumption, investment, the exchange rate and hence net exports.
Expansionary policy in a recession, contractionary policy against inflation.
Strengths: incremental, reversible, free of political pressure, quick to implement.
Limitations: time lags, the liquidity trap and the zero lower bound, low confidence blunting the effect, conflict with other objectives.
diagrams: Money market showing the interest rate
hl: The money market: demand for and supply of money
Quantitative easing as a tool when rates hit the lower bound
topics.trap: Monetary policy cannot fix cost-push inflation without cutting output. Saying so is one of the most reliable evaluation points in Unit 3.

topics.title: Demand management — fiscal policy
essentials: Government revenue and expenditure; the budget outcome as deficit, surplus or balance; government (national) debt.
Expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy and their effect on AD.
Automatic stabilisers: progressive taxes and unemployment benefits damping the cycle without new decisions.
The multiplier magnifying any fiscal change.
Strengths: targeted, effective in deep recession, can build potential capacity through infrastructure.
Limitations: political constraints, time lags, crowding out, debt sustainability.
diagrams: Expansionary fiscal policy closing a deflationary gap
Contractionary fiscal policy closing an inflationary gap
hl: Calculating the multiplier and the resulting change in real GDP
Using the multiplier to size a fiscal intervention
topics.trap: A budget deficit is a yearly flow; national debt is the accumulated stock. A government can cut its deficit while its debt still rises.

topics.title: Supply-side policies
essentials: The aim: to increase potential output by shifting LRAS or the Keynesian AS right.
Market-based policies: labour market reform, deregulation, privatisation, trade liberalisation, incentive-related tax cuts.
Interventionist policies: investment in education and training, healthcare, infrastructure, research and development, and industrial policy.
Effects on growth, unemployment, inflation and the trade balance — potentially improving several objectives at once.
Limitations: long time lags, high cost, equity concerns from market-based reforms, uncertain outcomes.
diagrams: Supply-side policy on the Keynesian AS curve
topics.trap: Supply-side policies are the only ones that can lower inflation and unemployment together. That makes them a strong closing evaluation in almost any macro policy question.

topics.title: Benefits of international trade
essentials: Gains from trade: lower prices, greater choice, economies of scale, more competition, access to resources, faster growth.
Absolute and comparative advantage, and specialisation according to lower opportunity cost.
Limitations of the comparative advantage model: transport costs, assumed constant costs, factor immobility, ignoring externalities.
diagrams: Production possibilities curves illustrating comparative advantage
hl: Calculating opportunity costs from output or input data to identify comparative advantage
Deriving the terms of trade at which both parties gain
topics.trap: Comparative advantage rests on opportunity cost, not on who produces more. A country can hold absolute advantage in everything and still gain from trade.

topics.title: Types of trade protection
essentials: Tariffs: effect on price, domestic production, consumption, imports, government revenue, and welfare.
Quotas: quantitative limits, with the gain going to importers rather than the government.
Subsidies to domestic producers as protection.
Administrative barriers: standards, licensing, customs procedures.
In every case: identify winners (domestic producers, sometimes government) and losers (consumers, foreign producers, overall welfare).
diagrams: Tariff with government revenue and welfare loss
Quota with the quota rent identified
hl: Calculating from a tariff diagram: revenue, welfare loss, changes in domestic production, consumption and imports
Calculating the effects of a quota and of a subsidy
topics.trap: On a tariff diagram there are TWO welfare loss triangles — production inefficiency and consumption inefficiency. Shading only one loses the calculation mark.

topics.title: Arguments for and against trade control/protection
essentials: Arguments for: infant industry, national security, health and safety standards, environmental standards, anti-dumping, protecting employment, correcting a current account deficit, government revenue.
Arguments against: higher prices and less choice, loss of the gains from comparative advantage, protected inefficiency, retaliation and trade wars, damage to exporters.
Weighing them depends on time horizon, the industry, and the alternatives available.
topics.trap: The infant industry argument requires a credible exit. Protection with no timetable for removal becomes permanent inefficiency — say this and you have your evaluation.

topics.title: Economic integration
essentials: Preferential trade agreements, bilateral and regional.
Stages of integration: free trade area, customs union, common market, monetary union, full economic union.
Trade creation and trade diversion.
Advantages and disadvantages of monetary union, including the loss of independent monetary policy and exchange rate adjustment.
The World Trade Organization: role, and the limits of its power.
topics.trap: A customs union adds a common external tariff to a free trade area. Getting the ladder of stages in order is a straightforward mark you should never drop.

topics.title: Exchange rates
essentials: Floating rates determined by demand for and supply of a currency; appreciation and depreciation.
Determinants: trade flows, investment flows, interest rate differentials, speculation, relative inflation.
Fixed and managed exchange rate systems; devaluation and revaluation.
Effects of a change in the exchange rate on inflation, employment, growth and the current account.
Central bank intervention to influence the rate, and its limits.
diagrams: Foreign exchange market: appreciation and depreciation
Central bank intervention to maintain a fixed rate
hl: Calculating exchange rates and converting values between currencies
topics.trap: Label the axes 'price of currency A in terms of currency B' and 'quantity of currency A'. Unlabelled forex axes are the fastest way to lose the diagram marks in Unit 4.

topics.title: Balance of payments
essentials: Structure: the current account, the capital account, and the financial account.
Components of the current account: trade in goods, trade in services, primary income, secondary income.
Why the accounts must balance overall, so a current account deficit is matched by a financial account surplus.
Consequences of a persistent current account deficit and of a surplus.
Correcting a deficit: expenditure switching, expenditure reducing, and supply-side measures.
The Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve effect.
hl: Calculating the balance on the current account and its components from data
Applying the Marshall-Lerner condition
topics.trap: The Marshall-Lerner condition is that the sum of PED for exports and imports exceeds 1. Only then does depreciation improve the current account — which is exactly why the J-curve dips first.

topics.title: Sustainable development
essentials: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
The tension between economic growth and environmental sustainability.
Poverty as both cause and consequence of environmental degradation.
The Sustainable Development Goals as a framework and a measurement problem.
hl: Sustainability constraints on long-run growth
topics.trap: Sustainable development is broader than environmental protection — it includes economic and social sustainability. Treating it as only 'green' narrows your answer.

topics.title: Measuring development
essentials: Economic growth versus economic development: growth is a rise in output, development is a broader rise in well-being and freedom.
Single indicators: GDP and GNI per capita at PPP, health indicators, education indicators, energy and environment indicators.
Composite indicators: the Human Development Index and its three dimensions; the inequality-adjusted HDI; the Gender Inequality Index.
Strengths and limitations of every indicator, particularly averaging away distribution.
topics.trap: HDI combines income, health and education. A country can post strong GDP growth and a flat HDI — that gap is usually the most interesting thing to say.

topics.title: Barriers to economic growth and/or economic development
essentials: Poverty traps and low-income cycles of low saving, low investment and low productivity.

Economic barriers: rising economic inequality, lack of access to infrastructure and appropriate technology, low levels of human capital, dependence on primary exports, volatile commodity prices, adverse terms of trade, capital flight, indebtedness.
Political and social barriers: weak institutions, poor governance, corruption, unequal political power, gender inequality, lack of property rights.
How the barriers reinforce one another.
topics.trap: Name the mechanism, not the label. 'Corruption is a barrier' scores little; 'corruption raises the effective cost of investment, deterring FDI and lowering the capital stock' is analysis.

topics.title: Economic growth and/or economic development strategies
essentials: Trade strategies: import substitution, export promotion, trade liberalisation, diversification.
Market-based approaches: liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, attracting foreign direct investment.
Interventionist approaches: education, health, infrastructure, industrial policy.
Foreign aid (humanitarian, development, tied), multilateral development assistance, debt relief.
Institutional change: microfinance and mobile banking, women's empowerment, reducing corruption, property and land rights.
Strengths and limitations of each, and of market-oriented versus interventionist approaches overall.
Progress toward selected Sustainable Development Goals, compared across countries.
topics.trap: There is no universally best strategy — the top band belongs to answers that say what the right strategy depends on: the country's institutions, factor endowments and stage of development.
